It’s easy to prove that the total variation distance between P and Q can be bounded as follows: X X δ(P, Q) ≤ δ(P{v}∪Πv , Q{v}∪Πv ) + δ(PΠv , QΠv ), v v where, as above, Πv denotes the parents of v in the DAG, if any. The sub-additivity of total variation distance with respect to the neighborhoods of the DAG allows us to distinguish between P = Q and δ(P, Q) ≥  by running n tests, distinguishing P{v}∪Πv = Q{v}∪Πv vs δ(P{v}∪Πv , Q{v}∪Πv ) ≥ /2n, for all v. We output “P = Q” if and only if all these tests output equality. Importantly the distributions P{v}∪Πv and Q{v}∪Πv are supported on |{v} ∪ Πv | variables. Hence if our DAG has maximum in-degree d, each of these tests requires O(|Σ|(d+1)/2 n2 /2 ) samples. An extra O(log n) factor in the sample complexity can guarantee that each test succeeds with probability at least 1 − 1/3n, hence all tests succeed simultaneously with probability at least 2/3. Unfortunately the quadratic dependence of the sample complexity on n is sub-optimal. A natural approach to improve the sample complexity is to consider instead the Kullback-Leibler divergence between P and Q. Pinsker’s inequality gives us that KL(P ||Q) ≥ 2δ 2 (P, Q).
